opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Kenji. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything or campaign for anyone. Nothing you tell me today will be linked to your name. I'll read you five short pictures of how AI might change things over the next five years, and ask how you'd react to each.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine. I'll be direct with you. I ran tech companies for most of my career, I use these tools every day, and I invest in AI start-ups. I think it should be moving faster than it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to other investors or online, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a missed chance. People were too cautious, regulators were too slow, and we settled for a fancy search box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of my start-ups would fail. I'd lose money, though nothing I can't afford. Mostly I'd be disappointed. I think the technology is better than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, with your money and your time? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut the weaker investments, back the two or three teams with real products. Spend more time with my wife, maybe travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frustrated. Bored, almost.

S0.say: It was a missed chance, with people too cautious and regulators too slow.
S0.think: Some of his start-ups would fail at an affordable loss, but mostly he'd be disappointed because he thinks the technology is better.
S0.do: Cuts weaker investments, backs the two or three teams with real products, and spends more time travelling with his wife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it to other investors or online, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tech is ready and the institutions aren't. Ten years is too slow. Get out of the way and let companies adopt it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My investments would do fine over time. But I'm 66. I'd like to see what this can do while I'm still around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, with your money and your time? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put money into companies that help big firms adopt AI faster. Mentor a couple of founders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Impatient. Not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not worried. Does the part about companies hiring fewer beginners bother you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. People adapt. I started in a world without the internet and I adapted. Young people are better at it than we were.

S1.say: The tech is ready and the institutions aren't, so they should get out of the way.
S1.think: His investments would do fine over time, but at 66 he wants to see what AI can do while he's around.
S1.do: Invests in companies that help big firms adopt AI faster and mentors a couple of founders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it to other investors or online, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what progress looks like. Some jobs go, new ones come. The worst thing politicians could do is panic and regulate it to death.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very good for me. My portfolio would grow a lot. I don't lose sleep over the layoffs, honestly. Companies should be run well, and people retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, with your money and your time? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put more into the start-ups building these assistants. Maybe fund a retraining company, because that's a market too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Energised, actually.

S2.say: This is what progress looks like, and politicians panicking into heavy regulation would be the worst outcome.
S2.think: His portfolio would grow a lot, and he doesn't lose sleep over layoffs because people can retrain.
S2.do: Invests more in start-ups building AI assistants and considers funding a retraining company as a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it to other investors or online, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains are real and they'll spread through cheaper goods and services. Taxing success to pay people not to work is a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? I'd be extremely rich. My worry is the politics. A crisis over who gets the gains usually ends with people like me getting a big tax bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, with your money and your time? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take some money off the table, spread it across countries. Talk to my lawyers about tax. Keep backing founders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Watchful about the politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the gains would spread. But you also expect a political crisis. Why would there be one, if they spread?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because spreading takes time and people are angry now. I understand the anger. I just don't think the answer is to take it from the people who built things.

S3.say: The gains will spread through cheaper goods and services, and taxing success to pay people not to work is a mistake.
S3.think: He'd be extremely rich, and his worry is a political crisis ending in a big tax bill for people like him.
S3.do: Takes some money off the table, spreads it across countries, consults his lawyers on tax and keeps backing founders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it to other investors or online, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest jump in what humans can produce in history. We'll have to work out the politics, but don't stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots I'm less close to, but I'd invest. What bothers me is unrest. When everyone's work is threatened at once, things can get ugly, and money doesn't protect you from a broken society.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, with your money and your time? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Invest in robotics. And, if I'm honest, think about where we live and how secure it is. Maybe give money to some kind of transition fund, on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about money. About people getting angry.

S4.say: This is the biggest jump in human productivity in history; the politics must be worked out, but it shouldn't be stopped.
S4.think: He'd invest in robots, but with everyone's work threatened at once he fears unrest that money can't protect him from.
S4.do: Invests in robotics, reconsiders where he lives and how secure it is, and may fund a transition scheme on his own terms.
S4.feel: Uneasy about people's anger, not money.
